# Sub-federal immigration policy in the 19th century

}}
Sub-federal immigration policy in the 19th century was common because the federal government had yet to establish its authority over migration. The main states involved in passing laws pertaining to immigration were coastal states because they received the most immigrants. However, by the end of the 1800s interior states were starting to want intervention by the government concerning immigration which led to increased federal involvement in the issue.
Immigration to the United States began to increase substantially in the mid-nineteenth century which led to citizens of coastal states bearing larger burdens of supporting poor migrants and increased uprisings against foreign born residents.
Irish immigrants were arriving in large numbers on the East Coast and Chinese immigrants were arriving on the West Coast which led to different reactions on either side of the continental United States. Eastern states, like Massachusetts, New York, Michigan, and North Carolina, took matters into their own hands and passed their own laws to regulate incoming migrants. However, states to the west did not pass as much legislation and relied more on local action and vigilantes.
Immigrant nationality
There were a variety of immigrant nationalities that arrived in the United States in the 1800s, but Irish and Chinese immigrants were two large groups that led to panic among American citizens and increased prejudice against foreign born residents.
Irish immigrants
The 1845-1852 potato famine in Ireland pushed many poor Irish off the island and searching for a new place to call home. Thousands of Irish immigrated into the United States (many poor and illiterate) who were looking for new opportunities. Many Irish were coming sick due to the starvation and many diseases that were occurring in Ireland which led to many needing to be hospitalized upon their arrival. Because of immigrants reliance on public help, many American citizens felt like they were being taken advantage of which led to states creating immigration laws to satisfy the demands of the people. Many of the states that implemented these policies were New England states because that is where a majority of Irish immigrants were landing.
Passenger cases
It was expensive to take care of the new immigrants because of the increased care many of them needed. Passenger brokers were supposed to pay bonds to the state in which they were docking to support their passengers. Many passenger brokers did not which increased the burden of the Irish on the American citizens who occupied cities where the Irish were landing. This issue eventually led to the case Smith v. Turner in New York and Norris v. City of Boston in Massachusetts; collectively known as the passenger cases. These cases established that portions of the laws that required taxes upon each immigrant entering into those states were unconstitutional and was some of the first restrictions put on states regarding immigration law.
Chinese immigrants
Chinese immigrants were the target of the first federal immigration policy in the United States in 1882, but that was sparked by local and state policies trying to limit immigration and limit racial violence. Immigrants from China came to the Western United States for a chance to strike gold in California, work on the railroad, and escape rough times in China. Chinese immigrants were considered unable to assimilate into American culture and were subject to many acts of persecution and removal because of that prejudice. Vigilantes were the main executors of excluding the Chinese before federal involvement (and many were still employed after the Chinese Exclusion Act to enforce the law).
The Californian government passed many laws and statutes that were later challenged by the US Supreme Court in cases like Chy Lung v. Freeman in 1875. California also instituted its Anti-Coolie Act of 1862 which required Chinese immigrants to pay a tax if they were not employed or working in certain industries. Legislation like this led to increased prejudice against Chinese immigrants which eventually led to federal legislation on the matter and led to many realizing that the best way to regulate immigration would be to enact it on the federal level.
State immigration policies
Coastal states were the main governments to pass immigration legislation because they were receiving most of the immigrants during the 19th century. Until the late 1800s, interior states did not have to worry about migration because most work was on the coast.
Massachusetts
Unlike how the federal immigration laws regulated the movement of people from other countries, Massachusetts state immigration laws, prior to the federal legislation, limited how "aliens" could move through and obtain property. During the mid-nineteenth century, much of the states laws, being intertwined with the public poor relief institutions, made difficult the immigration of the undesirable, free black slaves, Irish immigrants, and Chinese migrants movement into Massachusetts. Having access to the coast, they could refuse the arrival of incoming migrant ships if they believed it would be detrimental to the local economy.
In 1820, Massachusetts passed a series of Pauper and Alien acts that required ship captains to pay $500 for every migrant who did not have a settlement with the Massachusetts commonwealth. Prior to the Civil War, Massachusetts required the captains of these immigrant ships to include reports of the character and condition of every immigrant on board. If they were determined to be dissolute, or even one who abandoned life and character, they were not to be allowed in the state. Due to the influx of oncoming immigrants, the state of Massachusetts, as well as New York, put a large tax upon those migrants the reports deemed as not as desirable. This would later be challenged by the federal government in the 1849 passenger cases. A court case of the federal government that regarding the tax on these immigrant ships would be published and publicly accessible. The court case outlines the amounts of money the Port of Boston and New York had on these passenger cases, and lays out the attempt to heavily regulate the coming of immigrant ships. The supreme court would accuse the states with acting with sovereign power, going against the established constitution. Massachusetts would even go as far as publicly condemning certain voyages based on their immigrants. In the eyes of the state of Massachusetts, there was little to no difference between an immigrant coming over from halfway around the world, and an immigrant coming from the next state over.
New York
Original New York Laws established that one who remained in the state needed "legal settlement" or else they would be removed. These laws were later revised to better handle poor immigrants and to deter them from migrating to New York, but they did not work. New York received over 100,000 immigrants in 1846 alone and was not equipped to handle the number of people needing care after their rough journey and the poor circumstances of their previous home. The Port of New York was one of the busiest for newcomers in the 19th century which prompted many citizens of New York to push for regulation that was more suited for the change in migration flow. In order to handle large groups of immigrants, New York passed an act in 1847 establishing the Commissioners of Emigration which established that newcomers were eligible for public aid. It was the Commissioners of Emigration in New York that passed laws requiring bonds from certain types of passengers that led to the 1849 passenger cases that went to the U.S. Supreme Court and Henderson v. Mayor of New York that labeled such bonds unconstitutional.
The Commissioners of Emigration in New York were not hostile to immigrants and wanted to find humane ways to manage high migrant numbers which was different from many nativists of the day. They established regulations that improved conditions on the vessels that immigrants were traveling on, shortened the travel time, connected newcomers with their family and friends already present in the states, etc. However, there were many times when supply exceeded demand when it came to laborers.
The German Society and the Irish Emigrant Society were welfare organizations that also helped immigrants find jobs and protect migrants. These two societies were very important especially because the Irish and Germans were a large part of the incoming migration. The work of the German Society and the Irish Emigrant Society allowed for a lighter load on the state as they helped to care for poorer immigrants. However, this mattered less as the number of immigrants arriving increased.
Michigan
After the commencement of the 1840s immigration era, efforts were made through state legislature to entice European immigrants into the state of Michigan, while denying citizenship to Black men and women. This was an effort to exclude them and other undesirable migrants from the state of Michigan. Due to the influx of Eastern United States migrants coming to Michigan, it was recorded in the 1900 US census that 57 percent of the states population were foreign born. Factors for this influx included the overpopulation of Europe, and the industrialization in Germany, which killed old occupations in favor of new ones. The state of Michigan claimed to want only laborers who came at "especial invitation", and wanted to exclude migrants such as blacks and Indians. The dual state policy which was held at the time in the 1840s and 1850s did well to exclude these groups from their state.
In 1835 and 1850, the state of Michigan and its presiding constitutions gave instant housing and even voting rights to white male migrants of European heritage while at the same time, denying them to freed black slaves, enticing them to exit the state and to not settle there. For example, the state of Michigan, in the 1820s adopted a set of laws from the state of Ohio referred to as the Black Laws of 1804 and 1807. Laws like these and others made it very difficult for freed Black individuals to settle in the state. As a result, they were influenced to migrate out of the state to seek other means of settlement in other places.
Southern States
Immigration policy in the Southern United States was mostly in place to regulate the migration of free and enslaved Black people. States like South Carolina, Georgia, and North Carolina wrote legislation in the 18th century that prohibited migration of Black people from the Caribbean because they were concerned about an uprising among enslaved individuals. The Southern States eventually lobbied for federal regulation and were able to get Congress to pass laws regarding migration of Black people.
Deportation/detention
The Federal Government of the United States did not take full control of immigration policy until the latter half of the nineteenth century. Even today, cases such as Arizona v. United States are a modern representation of how states were involved in the immigration policy and deportation process back before the 1891 Immigration Act. On a state level, "Immigration Policy" decided what rights and privileges migrants had within their respective state. The majority of states shared views on migrant classes that they wanted to exclude from their states. These included free Black Americans, the poor, disabled bodied, and convicted migrants from Europe.
Both in practical application and in the application of law and policy, States within the nation deployed policies and various statutes that prevented the immigration of convicts and even the diseased from entering the State.
During the early 1800s most migrants who came to the United States came to New York City; specifically to Ellis Island. Once arriving, migrants would describe the place to be "grim," not like the promises that they had heard American offered. In fact, immigrants would go on to say that after each gate they passed through, they would feel "more cut off from life." Ellis Island was not just a checkpoint for migrants to get into America, it was also a prison for migrants. The island would often be used to filter out migrants who were more or less undesirable. Due to the high anti-Chinese sentiment, officers at Ellis Island and other local town leaders throughout the state would exclude Chinese workers.
Prior to the federal takeover of immigration in the late nineteenth century, state and local leaders were at the heads of many deportation and detention events. Not all deportations were done before formal hearings, as they are in formal deportations. "Self-Deportation Campaigns" as well as voluntary departures were methods of deportation and detention where the leaders of local town and state governments would use fear and other scare tactics to make life difficult for non-desirable migrants. This would cause migrants to voluntarily choose to leave the state, and in some cases, leave the country. local town leaders in the west such as Charles Fayette McGlashan would be a leading figure in the Anti-Chinese sentiment and enacting these sort of state deportations and self-deportation campaigns in the mid to late nineteenth century.
Naturalization
Naturalization has been a part of immigration for centuries. Naturalization during the late eighteenth and early nineteenth century was a well used social construct that played a heavy roll in facilitating territorial expansion and Native American integration in the United States, as well as immigration. Naturalization was a way of cementing loyalty to the United States and the pursuit of it economic and rural growth. Before the federal government took responsibility for the naturalization ceremonies that we know today, they were held by the states in court houses. In the 1780s, the state of Pennsylvania would have a court house magistrate make a migrant swear loyalty to the country, sign a paper, and with that, naturalization took only minutes. That is, if the state approved the ceremony based on the immigrants economic and social performances within the state. Just as it was with excluding migrants, naturalization was often reserved for those who were seen as a benefit to the overall performance of the state.
